questions.stem: Before psychological research with human participants can begin, it must be approved by:
questions.explanation: An ethics committee reviews research proposals to make sure they meet ethical guidelines, and monitors the conduct of the research. Research cannot start without its approval.

questions.stem: A researcher explains the procedure, risks and purpose of a study, and participants sign a form agreeing to take part. This addresses:
questions.explanation: Informed consent means participants agree to take part after being told what the study involves, including any risks. For participants under 18, a parent or guardian also gives consent.

questions.stem: Halfway through a study, a participant feels uncomfortable and leaves without penalty. Which ethical guideline allows this?
questions.explanation: Withdrawal rights allow participants to leave a study at any time, and to withdraw their data, without penalty. Voluntary participation is about agreeing to take part without pressure in the first place.

questions.stem: At the end of a study, the researcher explains its true purpose, corrects any false beliefs and checks participants are not distressed. This is:
questions.explanation: Debriefing occurs after participation: the researcher explains the aims and results, corrects any deception and makes sure participants leave without harm. It is essential when deception has been used.

questions.stem: Deception may be used in psychological research only when:
options: the study involves animals rather than human participants
knowing the aim would bias results and debriefing follows
participants have already given their names and contact details
the researcher wants to save time explaining the procedure
questions.explanation: Deception is acceptable only if revealing the aim would bias results, it will not cause harm, and participants are fully debriefed afterwards.

questions.stem: Results are stored with participants identified only by codes, and no names are published. This protects participants':
questions.explanation: Confidentiality means participants' personal information is kept secure and not disclosed, so they cannot be identified from published results.

questions.stem: Students are told that taking part in a teacher's study will earn them bonus marks, and those who decline will lose marks. Which guideline is breached?
questions.explanation: Voluntary participation means people take part freely, without pressure or coercion. Threatening to remove marks pressures students to participate.

questions.stem: A researcher uses fewer animals by improving the statistical design of a study. Which principle of animal research does this apply?
questions.explanation: Reduction means using the minimum number of animals needed for valid results. Replacement uses alternatives to animals, and refinement changes procedures to minimise pain and distress.

questions.stem: The variable that the researcher manipulates in an experiment is the:
questions.explanation: The independent variable is deliberately changed by the researcher to see its effect on the dependent variable, which is measured.

questions.stem: A researcher tests whether background music affects the number of words students recall from a list. The dependent variable is:
options: the length of the word list
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured to see the effect of the independent variable. Here, word recall is measured, and the music condition is the independent variable.

questions.stem: In a memory experiment, some participants are much more tired than others. Tiredness is an example of which kind of extraneous variable?
questions.explanation: Participant variables are characteristics of the participants, such as tiredness, age or motivation, that could affect the dependent variable. Environmental variables relate to the setting.

questions.stem: An extraneous variable becomes a confounding variable when it:
options: has no effect on the dependent variable at all
varies with the IV and also affects the DV
is kept the same for all participants throughout the study
is measured by the researcher as the main outcome of the study
questions.explanation: A confounding variable has affected the dependent variable in a way that cannot be separated from the effect of the independent variable, often because it differed between groups.

questions.stem: Which is a directional hypothesis?
options: Does the amount of sleep affect how many words students recall?
How do students describe their sleep before an exam?
Students who sleep 8 hours will recall more words than those who sleep 5
There will be a difference in recall between students who sleep 8 or 5 hours
questions.explanation: A directional hypothesis predicts the direction of the effect (more words recalled). A non-directional hypothesis predicts only a difference, and the questions are inquiry questions.

questions.stem: A researcher interviewing students about their experience of exam stress would usually guide the research with:
questions.explanation: Qualitative research explores experiences in depth, so it is guided by an inquiry question rather than a hypothesis that predicts a measurable result.

questions.stem: A researcher measures hours of social media use and wellbeing scores in 200 students, without manipulating any variable. This design is:
questions.explanation: A correlational study measures two variables as they occur naturally to see whether they are related. No variable is manipulated, so cause and effect cannot be concluded.

questions.stem: Researchers follow the same group of children from age 5 to age 18, testing their memory every two years. This design is:
questions.explanation: A longitudinal study follows the same participants over a long period, measuring changes over time. A cross-sectional study compares different groups at one point in time.

questions.stem: Which is the main advantage of a cross-sectional study over a longitudinal study?
options: It is quick, comparing different age groups at one time
It tracks the same people's development over many years
It removes all differences between the groups being compared
It allows cause-and-effect conclusions about age
questions.explanation: A cross-sectional study collects data from different groups at a single point in time, so it is quick and cheaper. Differences between groups may reflect their different life experiences rather than age itself.

questions.stem: An in-depth study of one person with a rare brain injury is a:
questions.explanation: A case study investigates a single individual or small group in great depth. It gives rich detail but its findings may not generalise to the wider population.

questions.stem: A researcher watches and records children's play in a school playground without interfering. This design is:
questions.explanation: An observational study records behaviour as it naturally occurs, without manipulating variables. It gives realistic data but cannot show cause and effect.

questions.stem: In a study of Year 12 students in Western Australia, the Year 12 students who actually take part are called the:
questions.explanation: The population is the whole group of interest (all Year 12 students in WA). The sample is the smaller group selected from it to take part.

questions.stem: A researcher asks students in her own class to take part because they are easy to reach. This sampling method is:
questions.explanation: Convenience sampling uses people who are readily available. It is quick and cheap but likely to be unrepresentative of the population.

questions.stem: To study people who have recovered from a rare illness, a researcher asks each participant to refer others they know with the same experience. This is:
questions.explanation: Snowballing recruits participants through referrals from existing participants. It is useful for hard-to-reach groups but the sample may share similar characteristics.

questions.stem: A school is 60% female and 40% male. A researcher selects a sample with the same proportions, choosing randomly within each group. This is:
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups (strata) and samples each in the same proportion as the population. It is more representative than simple random sampling for key characteristics.

questions.stem: Why is random allocation used in experiments?
options: to ensure participants do not know the aim of the study
to ensure that every participant receives the treatment
to spread participant variables evenly across the groups
to make the sample represent the population
questions.explanation: Random allocation gives each participant an equal chance of being in any group, so participant variables are likely to be spread evenly. Random sampling, not allocation, helps a sample represent the population.

questions.stem: Participants who take a sugar pill believing it is a memory-boosting drug improve their recall. This is the:
questions.explanation: The placebo effect is a change in behaviour or response caused by a participant's belief about a treatment, not by the treatment itself.

questions.stem: A researcher who expects one group to perform better unknowingly gives that group more encouragement. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The experimenter effect is an unintended influence of the researcher's expectations or behaviour on participants' responses. A double-blind procedure helps prevent it.

questions.stem: In a double-blind procedure:
options: participants choose for themselves which group they join
neither participants nor data collectors know the group allocation
only the participants do not know which group they are in
only the researcher does not know which group each participant is in
questions.explanation: In a double-blind procedure, neither participants nor the researchers interacting with them know the group allocation, which controls both the placebo effect and the experimenter effect. A single-blind procedure hides it only from participants.

questions.stem: Participants work out the aim of a study and change their behaviour to give the researcher the results they think are wanted. This is:
questions.explanation: Demand characteristics are cues that help participants guess the aim, leading them to change their behaviour. Single-blind procedures and some deception can reduce them.

questions.stem: Giving every participant the same written instructions in the same room at the same time of day is an example of:
questions.explanation: Standardised procedures and instructions make sure all participants have the same experience apart from the independent variable, reducing environmental and researcher extraneous variables.

questions.stem: Which of the following would count as qualitative data?
options: a participant's description of feeling anxious
a heart rate of 82 beats per minute
a score of 4 on a 5-point rating scale
the number of words recalled from a list
questions.explanation: Qualitative data are descriptions in words, such as feelings and experiences. Heart rates, scale scores and word counts are numerical, so they are quantitative.

questions.stem: Galvanic skin response (GSR) measures changes in the skin's electrical conductivity due to sweating. It is an example of:
questions.explanation: GSR is a physiological response measured by equipment, so it is objective and not influenced by the participant's interpretation. It is often used as an indicator of arousal.

questions.stem: Participants rate the statement 'I feel calm before exams' from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). This is a:
questions.explanation: A Likert scale asks participants to rate their agreement with statements. The scores are quantitative but subjective, because they depend on each participant's self-report.

questions.stem: A researcher interviews participants with a set list of core questions but asks follow-up questions depending on the answers. This is:
questions.explanation: A semi-structured interview combines planned questions with flexibility to explore answers further. A structured interview uses the same fixed questions in the same order for everyone.

questions.stem: Five students recalled 4, 6, 7, 9 and 14 words. What are the mean and median?
questions.explanation: The mean is the total divided by the number of scores: 40 / 5 = 8. The median is the middle score when ordered, which is 7.

questions.stem: A Pearson's correlation coefficient of r = -0.85 between hours of screen time and hours of sleep indicates:
options: that screen time causes less sleep
questions.explanation: Values close to -1 show a strong negative relationship: as one variable increases, the other decreases. Correlation alone cannot show that one variable causes the other.

questions.stem: Which correlation coefficient shows the strongest relationship between two variables?
questions.explanation: Strength depends on how close r is to +1 or -1, regardless of sign. At -0.72, this is the strongest; the sign only shows the direction.

questions.stem: Which graph is most suitable for showing the relationship between two continuous variables measured in each participant?
questions.explanation: A scatterplot shows each participant as a point plotted by their scores on two variables, revealing any correlation. Column graphs compare categories such as group means.

questions.stem: Internal validity refers to the extent to which a study:
options: produces the same results when repeated later
has results that apply to people outside the sample
has two observers who agree in their ratings of behaviour
tests what it claims to, so DV changes are due to the IV
questions.explanation: Internal validity is about whether the study actually tests what it set out to, with changes in the dependent variable caused by the independent variable rather than extraneous variables.

questions.stem: Two researchers independently score children's aggression from the same video and their scores closely agree. This shows high:
questions.explanation: Inter-rater reliability is the consistency of scores between different observers or raters. Test-retest reliability is consistency when the same test is repeated over time.

questions.stem: A study of 20 male university students in Perth finds that a memory technique works. Which is the main threat to external validity?
options: The results were measured with numbers
The sample may not represent the wider population
The memory technique was not given a name
The students were tested in the same city
questions.explanation: External validity is the extent to which results can be generalised beyond the study. A small, all-male student sample may not represent other ages, genders or groups.
